courts to encourage the States and High Courts to implement with enthusiasm. The
recognition can be in the line of Lok Adalat Court system recognised by Parliament
enactment to be manned by retired Judge, laymen other members of the court with powers
under Chapter VI and VI (A) of National Legal Services Authorities Act 1987. Moreso
mediation, conciliation and arbitration are the tools for success in that system with no
appeals to higher courts. Till tribal law is matured enough to be codified these tools will be
at the disposal of the Customary tribal courts. Criminal code, and Civil code can be
amended by concerned State Governments. When this committee recommended to establish
separate High Courts for North Eastern States in Twenty Sixth Report on Demands for
Grants (2008-09) of Ministry of Law and Justice presented to Parliament on 29th April,
2008, the then Government was hesitant since tribal judicial system may not allow to have
enough cases for the High Court. But Meghalaya High Court has recently suggested to the
to Committee to increase the number of Judges of that Court from 2 to 3 as huge pendency
of cases are to be cleared. Hence the tribal justice system has to be allowed to be
synchronised with regular Justice system at the root level so that judge-made law will give
energy to bring statutory law.      (Para 29)
12

13
3. The Committee notes that the main reasons for the avoidance of regular judicial
system by the tribal people in certain pockets of the country is due to expensive, lengthy
and confusing procedural laws and lengthy procedures of the regular Courts. The
Committee feels that non exposure of large number of tribal people to regular justice
system has forced large number of them to remain out of the ambit of mainstream justice
delivery system prevailing in the country. The Committee while recognising the contribution
of customary practices of tribes in dispensation of justice, feels that benefits of regular
justice system should not be denied to tribal people. (Para 30)
4. The Committee strongly feels that the respective State Governments have to initiate
the process of synergising the two. Firstly, they have to allay the apprehension from the
minds of the people that they would lose the benefits of tribal justice system and  instil the
faith that it would rather strengthen it. Secondly, they should also make available the
necessary infrastructure, competent and trained judicial officers through its judicial
academies, and also by introducing modern record management practices. The services of
State Legal Services Authorities at States and Districts level may be utilised in the region to
remove the skepticism and reservations among the tribal people in the region about the
regular justice system. The Committee is not at all for replacement of customary justice
delivery mechanism with the regular system but is of the view that these two systems
instead of being compartmentalised should converge in a symbiotic manner to enhance
access to justice to those indigenous inhabitants. (Para 31)
5. The Committee observes that in contrast to the general perception of egalitarian
nature of tribal societies, women in many tribal societies are not permitted to participate in
public offices and their property rights are also restricted. The Committee feels that
representation of women in the tribal bodies and district councils may be encouraged by
consultation and legislative process to bring gender equality in the local administration as
provided under the Part IX of the Constitution in the Panchayat Raj Inst itutions. (Para 32)
6. The Committee observes that at present there are large bodies of tribal laws which
are oral in tradition and transmitted from generation to generation. A few attempts have
been made in Nagaland among Ao and Zelang Tribes  and in Assam among Bodos to document
and codify their customary laws. The Committee also recognises the efforts of Law
Research Institute, Guwahati in documenting customary law in the North-East region. The
Committee feels that such efforts need to be encouraged in the region for documentation
and finally codification of diverse customary laws prevalent among various tribes in the
region. The Committee is of the view that a careful examination of the similarities/
dissimilarities between the regular and tribal justice system of the country is the need of
the hour so that the tribal laws can be documented and codified and a synergy can be
brought with the regular justice system as oral traditions sometimes leads to arbitrary
dispensation of justice and violates the principle of natural justice and rights provided under
the Constitutional of India.  This can be undertaken in the project Access to Justice for
North-East and Jammu and Kashmir which is currently being implemented by Department
of Justice. (Para 33)
7. The Committee feels that efforts can also be made to provide training and building

14
capacities of traditional/customary judicial officials, Gaon Buras , Cheirups , Dobashish  etc. on
the principles of natural justice in the State Judicial Training Academies. The Committee
feels that training and infrastructure should be provided to State Judicial Academies to train
tribal leaders, chief of Gaon Buras  etc.  so as to apprise them of the benefits of regular
justice system and integrate them to regular justice system of the Country, ultimately,
bringing about a synergy between both these systems for the development and good
governance of Tribal Areas in the country. The financial implications of these training
programmes and empowerment activities need to be worked  out by the respective
authorities.  (Para 34)
8. As per the Government of India (Allocation of Business) Rules, 1961, administration
of justice, access to justice, justice delivery system  and legal aid to poor falls under the
purview of Department of Justice, Ministry of Law and Justice and Tribal Welfare,
Development of Scheduled Tribes and Scheduled Areas falls under the purviews of the
Ministry of Tribal Affairs. The Committee during its deliberations with the Departments and
Ministries of the Government of India on the subject observed that the issue of tribal
justice system in the country has not been taken seriously by the Department of Justice or
Ministry of Tribal Affairs for the reason that the issue does not specifically fall within their
domain as per (Allocation of Business) Rules, 1961. The Committee feels that at apex level
it is the Department of Justice endowed with the responsibility of administration of justice
and accordingly expect that department to initiate the process of synergising both the
justice delivery systems and coordinate with the concerned State Governments, Tribal
Councils and other stakeholders. (Para 35)
9. The Committee in its Twenty Sixth Report on Demands for Grants (2008-09) of
Ministry of Law and Justice, presented to Parliament on 29th April, 2008 had recommended
for establishing separate High Courts for North Eastern States which will in turn play the
role of evolving codification of the tribal laws. It had felt that such a step would ensure that
the judgements of the High Courts will be treated as precedents, which with passage of
time, can evolve into written law. The interpretations given to the existing uncodified rules/
laws by the High Courts, can in future, be consolidated and this will result in codified laws
and uniformity of judgements. This Committee now reiterates that all the North Eastern
States should have separate High Courts and independent Judicial Academy should be
established in every State to fulfil the real goal of synchronisation of Tribal Justice system
with the National mainstream of unitary Judicial system which is the architecture of Indian
Constitution. (Para 36)

provide for administration of tribal areas in notified States. Special Constitutional provisions under

Committee that the Secretary, Ministry of Tribal Affairs and some non-official witnesses have been
invited to depose on the subject 'Synergy between Tribal Justice System and Regular Justice

3. Chairman in his opening remarks observed that Ministry of Tribal Affairs is concerned with
tribal issues in general and their input on the subject could be extremely beneficial for the
Committee. Disputes may arise while conferring tenurial land rights to tribals under the Forest
Rights Act, 2006, and disputes resolution mechanism under the said Act has been provided.
Referring to Committee's visit to North-Eastern States, Chairman mentioned that village head need
financial assistance for discharging their duty as an adjudicator between tribals.  The Committee
felt that setting up of judicial academies, exclusive High Courts in all the North Eastern States
would help to recognize customary tribal laws in these States.  Thereafter, Secretary, Tribal Affairs
made a presentation supplemented by his Joint Secretary.
4. The Secretary submitted that the Forest Rights Act basically relates to customary land rights
of tribals and has nothing to do with tribal justice system. He averred that Ministry of Tribal Affairs
is essentially concerned with governance issues in tribal area under Fifth Schedule of the
Constitution. He added that as per Allocation of Business Rules, 1961 administration of justice,
access to justice and justice delivery system are allocated to Department of Justice. The subject
matter of synergy between tribal justice system and regular justice system in the country is
subsumed under that mandate. There is neither a division nor any record of past experience with
the Ministry for dealing with the subject. Therefore, he opposed transfer of this subject to his
Ministry from Department of Justice.
5. The Joint Secretary in Ministry of Tribal Affairs added that Village Panchayat/Council of
Tribal communities residing in Fifth Schedule areas do not exercise judicial power while those
residing in Sixth Schedule areas have judicial powers. Since customary tribal laws are a sort of oral
tradition, codification thereof is a tough challenge for the State. There have been allegations that
village heads have reportedly used those customary laws prejudiciously in favour of their relatives
and acquaintances. He submitted that customary tribal law should be in conformity with principle
of natural justice and need to be synchronized with regular justice system to check its misuse.
6. Members pointed out that inspite of Forest Rights Act having overriding effect over other
existing laws, the Forest Department are coming in the way of implementation Forest Rights of
tribals.  The Tribal Village Panchayat have not been involved in the process. Tribal people cannot
mortgage their land resources to get bank loan for their economic development. The problem of
rehabilitation of displaced tribal population due to mining operation need to be looked into.

Shri John F. Kharshing, Co-Chariman, Meghalaya State Planning Board and Prof. Nandini Sundar,

8. Shri H.S. Thangkhiew, Advocate, submitted that three prominent tribes ( Khasi, Jaintias  and
Garos) inhabitating in the hills of Meghalaya have their age old system of dispute resolution where
the decisions are taken up by consensus from village level to the chief of the tribe.  Rules for the
Administration of Justice framed in 1937 had recognized the role of village councils/courts and
village headman in the dispensation of justice amongst tribes. The Constitution under Sixth Schedule
has given power to Autonomous District Councils for constituting village courts/councils for trial of
suits amongst tribes, appointment/succession village headman, tribal customs etc., for disposal of
cases between them. The Administration of Justice Rules enacted in 1953 also recognized village
courts, District Councils but those are not functioning properly due to lack of finance and
infrastructure.  He, therefore, suggested that financial resources may be granted to the District
Council by the State Government for making it vibrant. The Transfer of Property Act, Specific
Reliefs Act should be made applicable in the scheduled areas. Village headman should be given
training in judicial processes by the State to resolve disputes in judicious manner.
9. Shri John F. Kharshiing referred to the Instrument of Acession entered into between some
of the Khasi Chiefs and Government of India, but that has not been mentioned in the Constitution
of India. However, none of the Chiefs are part of legislature and they are dependent for legislation
on the District Council which is a party-based body whereas the Chiefs are partyless institutions.
He submitted that ninety percent people in Meghalaya register their land with the Chiefs and not in
accordance with the Indian Registration Act, 1908. About eighty percent of cases in Meghalaya
goes to District Council for redressal of their grievances but those lack financial resource and
infrastructure to deal with the burden of cases. On the issue of codification of customary laws, he
opined that sometimes there is a conflict between the customary laws and the regular justice
system and felt that there is a need for synergy between them.
10. Prof. Nandini Sundar submitted that situation in Sixth Schedule areas are much better than
the Fifth Scheduled areas as far as the preservation of traditional justice systems is concerned. The
Y ule Rules, Santhal Police Rules and Pargana Majhi Rules in tribal areas of Central India allow the
tribals some degree of autonomy to preserve customary laws. But implementation of Panchayats
(Extension to Scheduled Areas) Act 1996 (PESA) had eroded such system. She added that the
customary practices needed to be recognized and revived. She apprised the Committee of the denial
of rights to tribal women in the traditional and customary laws. She also added that the complicated
procedures of formal legal system pushes the Adivasis towards to legal system delivered by Maoist,
where the justice delivery is quick and effective.

REPORT
A. Introductory Observation:
Treaties are frequently described as contracts between nations. As instruments of
International law, they establish obligations with which International law requires the parties to
comply at national level as well as international level. Entering into treaties and agreements with
foreign powers is one of the attributes of State sovereignty. The Vienna Convention of Law of
Treaties is the main instrument that regulates treaties. Article 2(1)(a) of the Vienna Convention of
Law of Treaties defines treaties as an international agreement concluded between States in written
form and governed by International Law, whether embodied in a single instrument or in two or
more related instruments and whatever its particular designation. The doctrine of pacta sunt
servanda  contained in articles 26 and 27 of the Vienna Convention, 1980 which lays down that
every treaty in force is binding upon the parties to it and must be performed in good faith.
2. The Consultation Paper under the auspices of National Commission to Review the Working
of the Constitution on topic of “Treaty Making Power under Our Constitution” begins with the
note, “ Entering into treaties and agreements with foreign powers is one of the attributes of State
sovereignty. No State can insulate itself from the rest of the world whether it be in the matter of
foreign relations, trade, environment, communications, ecology or finance. This is more true since
the end of the World War II. The advent of globalisation and the enormous advances made in
communication and information technology have rendered independent States inter-dependent. Every
State has entered into and is entering into treaties – be it multi-lateral or bilateral – which have a
serious impact upon the economy and the social and political life of its society. In spite of the
fundamental importance of the treaty-making power, it has unfortunately received very little
attention in our country, though in many other countries, good amount of research and debate has
gone into it .” (January 8, 2001) The above mentioned specific topic under the National
Commission to Review the Working of the Constitution was headed by Hon’ble Justice Shri B. P.
Jeevan Reddy.
B. Current Practice of Entering into International Treaties and the Executing Agencies
3. Article 51 of the Constitution of India enjoins the State to endeavour to “ foster respect for
international law and treaty obligations in the dealings of organised peoples with one another ”. For
the purpose of international relations and international obligations, the ‘State’ referred to in Article
51 is understood to be the Union of India, i.e. the Central Government. According to the
Constitutional arrangements, in particular Entries 10 and 14 of List 1 of the Union List in the
Seventh Schedule of the Constitution, all matters of foreign affairs which bring the Union into
relation with foreign countries including entering into treaties and agreements fall within the ambit
of the Union of India, the Central Government.
4. Under the Government of India (Allocation of the Business) Rules, 1961, as per Rule 3 of
the Second Schedule regarding ‘Distribution of subjects among the Departments’, the Ministry of

2
External Affairs has been entrusted the responsibility to negotiate Political treaties, agreements and
conventions with foreign and Commonwealth countries in various disciplines and subjects which
inter alia  include:
 matters relating to Law of the Sea, including the Indian Territorial Waters,
Contiguous Zone, Continental Shelf and Exclusive Economic Zones (EEZ);
 questions of international law arising on the high seas including fishery rights; piracy
and crimes committed on the High Seas or in the air;
 offences against the Law of Sovereign States committed on land or the High Seas or
in the air;
 legal matters concerning the International Seabed Area and Authority;
 United Nations, Specialised Agencies and other International Organisations and
Conferences;
 extradition and laws relating to extraditing of accused persons from India to foreign
and commonwealth countries and vice versa;
 demarcation of the land frontiers of India;
 maritime boundaries of India;
 human Rights law including: (a) interaction with Human Rights abroad; (b)
international declarations, treaties, conventions and conferences; (c) references
received from the United Nations and other specialised agencies and organisations
thereof; (d) implementation of reporting obligations, in coordination with the
concerned Ministries, required under the United Nations and international
conventions, to which India is a State party.
4.1 The same Rules has also allocated the subject “Treaties and agreements with foreign
countries in matters of civil law” to the Department of Legal Affairs, Ministry of Law & Justice.
5. The Committee has been informed by the Ministry of External Affairs that for discharging
its allocated functions and responsibilities in this regard, the Ministry has created the Legal and
Treaties Division in 1957 which is entrusted with the work relating to public international law. The
Division is approached for private international law work/issues by other Ministries and deals with
cases before the International Court of Justice and international arbitrations as well. The Division
also advises MEA and other Ministries/Departments of the Government of India on all issues of
international law including negotiations of treaties and agreements; and vetting of bilateral and
multilateral treaties/Memorandums of Understanding from international law angle.
6. As regards the role of the Department of Legal Affairs, Ministry of Law and Justice, it has
informed the Committee that the Department is primarily concerned with tendering of advice to
Ministries on legal matters including interpretation of the Constitution and the laws and conduct of
cases in the Supreme Court and the High Courts on behalf of the Central Government and on
behalf of the Governments of States participating in the Central Agency Scheme. It is also
concerned with reciprocal arrangements with foreign countries for the service of summons in civil

3
suits for the execution of decrees of Civil Courts, for the enforcement of maintenance orders, and
for the administration of the estates of foreigners dying in India.
7. The Department of Legal Affairs and Legislative Department (Ministry of Law) are required
to be consulted as per the Transaction of Business Rules on all Legislative proposals before the

which legal opinion on questions of International Law or Treaties is sought by other Ministries
Departments in view of O.M.No.F.3(8)-O&M/61/1/152 dated the 30
th August, 1961 of the Ministry
of External Affairs which has requested that cases in which legal opinion on questions of
international law or treaties are required to be referred to the Legal and Treaties Division of the
Ministry of External Affairs.
8. The Department of Legal Affairs, however, in its advisory capacity is concerned with all
bilateral and multilateral treaties on legal issues and its impact on domestic law and examines the
Constitutional aspects irrespective of the subject allocation. The Department also examines issues
like clarity and formulation of provisions, legal implications of the Agreements, predominance of

Agreement. In the event of signing of any Treaty relating to the subjects related to different

9. In its written submission to the Committee, the Department of Legal Affairs has stated that
in number of instances, representatives of the Ministry of Law have not been involved at the time
of negotiating a draft Agreement and merely the negotiated draft Agreements were sent to this
Department for comments. It has suggested that representatives of the Department are made part
of the initial negotiations as well, so that legal implications of provisions are appropriately
understood and timely taken care of.
10. Whenever the Ministry of External Affairs comes across a situation while examining the
provisions of a Treaty that it has impact on the rights conferred by domestic law, it consults the
Department of Legal Affairs for opinion on the legal issues arising therein. The Department is also
consulted whenever in the process of negotiation or other matter with a foreign country involving
examination of any domestic legislation or any clarification on any domestic law issues with the
view of ensuring conformity with the relevant municipal laws and whenever any amendment in the
existing municipal law or an implementing legislation is required to fulfil the obligations assumed
under any international treaty/agreement.
C. Trends in Some Democratic Countries
11. In the United Kingdom, a practice was established whereby any treaty subject to ratification
is laid before Parliament for at least 21 sitting days before ratification is carried out, though
ratification being an executive power. Article II, Section 2 of the U.S. Constitution empowers the
President “ by and with the advice and consent of the Senate, to make treaties, provided two-thirds
of the Senators present concur … ”. The President initiates and conducts negotiations of the treaties

4
and after signing them, places them before Senate for its “Advice and Consent”. In Australia,
treaties, both bilateral and multilateral are required to be tabled at least for 15 sitting days, after
signature but before they are ratified, to allow for parliamentary scrutiny. A joint Standing
Committee on treaties comprising Members of both Houses and consisting of Federal and State
Officers consider and report upon the treaties tabled before the House. The Canadian practice is
that, mandatory approval from the Parliament is required only in case of treaties that require
implementing legislation.
12. In New Zealand, the parliamentary treaty examination process introduced in 1997 and made
permanent in 2000 requires all multilateral treaties and major bilateral treaties of particular
significance to be presented to the House before binding treaty action is taken. In accordance with
the process, once Cabinet has approved the proposed treaty action, the Legal Division of the
Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Trade is responsible for presenting the treaty and the National
Interest Analysis to the House of the Representatives. Once a treaty has been presented, it stands
referred to the Foreign Affairs, Defence and Trade Committee of the House.
D. Mandate to Indian Parliament to Give Effect to Treaties
13. Article 253 the constitution has empowered the Parliament to give effect to international law
treaties for the whole or any part the territory of India and reads:
“253. Legislation for giving effect to international agreements notwithstanding anything in
the foregoing provisions of this Chapter, Parliament has power to make any law for the
whole or any part of the territory of India for implementing any treaty, agreement or
convention with any other country or countries or any decision made at any international
conference, association or other body .”
14. In Maganbhai Ishwarbhai Patel vs. Union of India [(2002) 3 SCC], the Supreme Court
observed that “A treaty really concerns the political rather than the judicial wing of the State.
When a treaty or an award after arbitration comes into existence, if has to be implemented and this
can only be if all the three branches of Government, the Legislature, the Executive and the
Judiciary, or any of them, possess the power to implement it. If there is any deficiency in the
Constitutional system it has to be removed and the State must equip itself with the necessary
power.” Justice J.C. Shah observed in the aforesaid decision that “the effect of Article 253 is that
if a treaty, agreement or convention with a foreign State deals with a subject within the competence
of the State Legislature, the Parliament alone has, notwithstanding Article 246(3), the power to
make laws to implement the treaty, agreement or convention or any decision made at any
international conference, association or other body. In terms, the Article deals with legislative
power: thereby power is conferred upon the parliament which it may not otherwise possess.”
15. India adopts dualistic approach in relation to Treaties/Conventions which regards
international law and municipal law are separate in which one does not prevail over the other. India
follows the British practice as it existed at the time of its independence. States’ obligation to
domesticate its valid international obligations can be drawn from the Permanent Court of
International Justice (PCIJ) decision on Exchange of Greek and Turkish Populations Case , PCIJ
Reports, Series B, No. 10 (1925), 20. Also Article 27 of Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties
to which India is not yet a party (to the Vienna Convention 1969) provides that national law cannot

5
be invoked to justify non-compliance with international law. This approach entrusted major role to
Indian Parliament to ensure the implementation of international law and also to protect national
interest. This approach led the Indian Parliament to harmonise the international aspiration vs national
interest.
16. In February, 2000, the Ministry of Law and Justice set up the National Commission to
Review the Working of the Constitution to recommend functional changes which could be made to
the Constitution and parliamentary system in the light of socio-economic developments. The
Consultation Paper of the Commission gave two principal suggestions, i.e., (i) the Parliament must
make a law to regulate the treaty making power and; (ii)  the Union Government must consult with
States prior to signing any treaty in order to reduce conflicts with State Governments. The Second
Commission on Centre-State Relation headed by former Chief Justice of India M.M. Punchhi
recommended in its report in March, 2010 that in view of the vast and plenary nature of the
power, the Parliament should enact a law  to streamline the procedures involved in treaty-making.
While acknowledging that treaty-making involved complex, prolonged, multi-level issues which
could only be well handled by the executive, the Commission nevertheless felt that “Constitutional
mandate on federal governance cannot be ignored” .
17. In India, the Executive has been taking action on giving effect to treaties under Article 73
read with Entries 10 and 14 of list I of Seventh Schedule of the Constitution while Article 253 of
the Indian Constitution has empowered the Parliament to make any law for the whole or any part
of the territory of India for implementing any treaty, agreement or convention with any other
country or countries or any decision made at any international conference, association or other
body. The Ministry of External Affairs of the Government of India also issued a notification no. 1/
13/2/2010-Cab dated 2011, whereby accession to or ratification of such convention/treaties, be
undertaken only after relevant domestic laws have been amended, or the enabling legislation has
been enacted in cases, where there are no domestic laws on the subject.
18. The Indian Society of International Law submitted that use of resources and expertise of
Parliament and that Indian Parliament has to be involved in such matters in order to permit the law
to evolve and to develop properly. Views have also been expressed that the involvement of
Parliament could reduce the risk of inconsistent body of laws and help to legitimise and
institutionalise the process of inclusion of international law into domestic law and would aid in
making the system sustainable. Some Members likewise endorsed this view.
18.1 The Ministry of External Affairs also, in its written submission, acknowledged that
Parliament continues to exercise exclusive power in cases where implementing legislation may be
necessary to give effect to treaties, which may necessitate the adoption of the necessary legislation
by the Parliament before the treaty in question may be ratified and that Parliament has necessary
oversight over the treaty-making power of the Union Government.
E. Indian Courts and International Law
19. There has been a tremendous increase in standard setting/law making of international law on
various subjects bearing direct implications on India’s national interest. In the absence of any
domestic law, many of the cases in the Supreme Court are now finding that the international

6
treaties, conventions and agreements are enforced as it is. The treaty law raises many difficult
issues concerning the proper balance to be found between the international law and Indian domestic
law. The general ‘proliferation’ and increasing importance of treaty law, inter-governmental
organisation, international courts and tribunals introduce both substantive and procedural obligations
on States. The numerous International Courts and tribunals are continuously interpreting the
existing international law principles and expect that a State including India has to comply with those
interpretations. This requires a dedicated State institution to ensure that its laws and practice give
effect to these interpretations or to bring the national law in accordance with interpretations
provided by complex regime of international courts and tribunals.
20. There has been a couple of recent high profile examples of what can only be described as
inconsistent decisions in national and international judicial bodies. Many are concerned with
fundamental issues, viz., impairment of the friendly relations with other nations, principle of
peaceful co-existence, obligation of State trading partners, breach of international duty,  providing
effective remedy for violations of human rights and rule of law, non-discrimination provisions in
the WTO, freedom of the seas, common heritage of mankind, common concern of mankind,
delimitation of seas, freedom of navigation, peaceful exploration of outer space, etc. In brief, there
are a plethora of issues arising in respect of the co-existence of municipal and international courts
and remedies stemming out from the complex web of international law regime and the ever-
growing number of legal proceedings, both at national and international levels brought by States/
individuals against another State. Therefore, the relationship between local courts and international
law to give effect to the international law obligations poses a challenge.
21. The Department of Legal Affairs has also submitted that treaties do not become part of
Municipal law and Courts in India cannot interpret them unless Parliament enacts a legislation by
exercising power conferred under Article 253 of the Constitution read with Entry 14 of the List I
of the Seventh Schedule to the Constitution in order to make it part of domestic law. As per the
existing norms, treaty is enforceable only when it is ratified by India after completing the
constitutional procedure.
22. The Supreme Court of India in Aban Loyd Chiles Offshore v. UOI (2008) 11 SCC 439)  held
that in the absence of municipal law, treaties can be looked into, if they are not in conflict with
municipal law. In Vishaka v. State of Rajasthan  ((1997) 6 SCC 241) and National Legal Services
Authority v. Union of India , ((2014) 5 SCC 438), the Supreme Court of India again applied
international law even when there was no municipal law. In T. N. Godavarman Thirumulpad v.
Union of India  ((2012) 4 SCC 362), the Supreme Court laid down a short but categorical directive
that treaties not contrary to municipal law are deemed to be incorporated in the municipal law. The
1969 and 1986 Vienna Conventions on the Law of Treaties between States and International
Organisations or between International Organisations mandate that their rules apply as binding
norms to the mutual relations entered into through Treaties/Covenants/Agreements.
23. There have been instances where Indian courts chose the random way in which questions
of international law are disposed of. In Xavier v. Canara Bank Ltd  (1969), the Kerala High Court
held that individual citizen could not complain about the breach of the International Covenants on
Human Rights in the municipal courts “ even if the country concerned has adopted the covenants
and ratified the Optional Protocol ”. At the time when this judgment was given, India was a party

7
to International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights (ICCPR) and International Covenant on
Economic, Social and Cultural Rights (ICESCR) which shows that the Court did not even evaluate
the difference between signing and ratification of treaties. In Biswambhar Singh v. Orissa  (1957),
the Orissa High Court observed that India is “ one of the parties to the Universal Declaration of
Human Rights ” which was a General Assembly resolution and does not require signature or
ratification process of a treaty.
24. April 2014 issue of ‘ UNCTAD IIA Issues Note’ indicated that by end of 2013, 98 States
have been respondents in a total of 568 known treaty-based cases which is indicative of the rising
trend of arbitration cases brought by States and international investors. The said report has also
indicated India as the eighth most frequent respondent State in 2013 with Czech Republic topping
the list.
F. India’s Role in International Law Making
25. The Ministry of External Affairs has informed the Committee that in recent years, the
approximate number of multilateral and bilateral treaties, agreements and memoranda of
understanding concluded annually is over three hundred on various subjects pertaining to different
administrative Ministries. All treaties and agreements that are in force and having the intention of
the States Parties to create legal obligations are binding and such treaties and agreements shall be
observed in good faith (pacta sunt servanda) . Approximately, around 3,500 treaties have been
concluded by India since 1950.
26. India is also a member of various international Dispute Settlement Bodies whose
responsibility is to determine disputes involved on the subject of the treaties. The presence of
competent experts on international law to represent in these bodies is bound to ensure the national
interest. It has, however, been observed that the Indian representations in some of the Dispute
Settlement Bodies has been minimal.

 As tax treaties are entered into by the Central Government under the provisions of
Section 90 of the Income-tax Act, 1961, which itself provides that the provisions of

these treaties.
 Tax treaties do not require any reporting to any international body.
 Tax treaties entered by India, as also by most other countries, do not provide for

country to collect taxes on income arising from its territory.

Recommendations/Observations of the Committee
47. The Committee observes that it has been the experience at international fora or at
the occasion of negotiating bilateral or multilateral treaties, the developed countries are
seen to be represented by large number of legal experts whereas Indian delegation is not
supported by matching number of legal experts. The Committee feels that our delegations
are not adequately equipped to that extent. The Committee wishes that at such occasions,
we should have equally capable negotiating team full of experts in domain and legal
knowledge with a view to instantly interpret provisions of negotiations and providing
alternative formula, if required, in the interest of the country.
48. The Committee observes that there is a need for creating a pool of experts in
various fields of the International Law to be drawn to different Departments/Organisations/
Institutions of the Government of India and the States in the capacity of legal advisors/
consultants, negotiators, experts in reporting in international fora and the multilateral and
bilateral talks. The Committee feels that such an institutional capacity will address the
immediate need of experts in the category of advisors, consultants, negotiators, drafting
experts in reporting in international fora and the multilateral/bilateral talks.
49. It feels that it is the need of the hour to streamline the existing mechanism of
handling all issues relating international co-operation and international legal obligations and
accordingly, recommends that the ‘Department of International Law’ may be created to
work as a nodal body to create a group of legal experts who will be serving the different
Ministries as and when it is required. This Department would be responsible to coordinate
and evolve specialised approach while negotiating any international convention or bilateral
or multilateral treaty. This process eventually would lead to involvement of legal experts as
well as domain experts from concerned Ministries at the fore-front of the negotiation

21
process and also accompanied by the officers of the Ministry of Law and Justice to advise on
the position of domestic law. The Department of International Law would have dual role i.e.,
ensuring the effective negotiations of treaties and its actual implementations at national
and international level. Finally, that Department would be able to develop a mechanism
providing for a more coherent, holistic and specialised approach among the state
institutions.
50. The Committee hopes that the newly created Department of International Law may
simultaneously develop the desired human resource, competent in matters relating to
international law, who may help the negotiators to develop a consistent approach on
international matters in international fora.
51. The Committee further observes that Department of International Law would be
repository of all the binding international Conventions, Bilateral/Multilateral treaties,
Resolutions and rules relating thereto.  The Department should also publish the same. This
would sensitise about the issues/subject involved to the country’s institutions and also the
people at large. The Department of International Law would further be mandated to bring
to the notice of all courts/tribunals in the country about the new interpretations given by
International Court(s) or Tribunals on any subject.
52. The Committee feels that it is now well settled that international law is no longer
limited to the regulation of diplomatic relations between States.  The gap between the
international courts and the domestic courts has now been substantially narrowed.  It,
therefore, calls for the incorporation of international norms into the national law as the
international law/rules/norms today aim at the matters which were earlier exclusively
belonged to the domestic jurisdiction of States and conversely, the domestic courts also deal
with the issues relating to international law.  The Committee accordingly feels that setting
up of this Department would be a step in filling up of the gap between the two.
53. Hence, the Committee recommends for setting up of a new Department of
International Law similar to the existing Department of Legal Affairs, Legislative
Department and Department of Justice.  The Ministry can be renamed as Ministry of
International Law, Domestic Law and Justice.
54. The Committee notes that as per existing practice, the Ministries/Departments have
the responsibility to implement India’s obligations in respect of the subjects pertaining to
them as per Government of India (Allocation of the Business) Rules, 1961. The Committee,
however, feels that it would certainly be in fitness of things that there is a need for creation
of a new ‘Department of International Obligations & Implementations’ under the direct
supervision of Prime Minister in the line of Department of Space, etc. The Committee feels
such a Department will provide for a monitoring mechanism at apex level and will further
strengthen the existing system. This would enhance the status of India in the community of
Nations as India aspires to be a Member of United Nations Security Council and also claims
to be an Economic Power.
55. It is further recommended that these two new Departments should be headed by
international law professionals and experts for a fixed term in the rank of Secretary aided

22
by Joint Secretary level officers from Indian Foreign Service, Indian Administrative Service,
other Central services and if needed, by the experts in the relevant fields who will co-
ordinate with various Departments and Ministry of External Affairs and Embassies/High
commissions.
56. The Committee recommends that the Ministry of External Affairs,  Ministry of Law
and Justice (to be rechristened as Ministry of International Law, Domestic Law and Justice)
and the concerned nodal Ministry designated for such negotiations should work as ‘Trinity’
in all negotiations of any bilateral/multilateral Treaties/International Conventions etc. The
Department of International Obligation & Implementation which may be under the direct
supervision of Prime Minister’s Office (PMO), as suggested above, is to work as overall
overseeing the working of the Trinity towards the implementation of  post-Treaty
obligations.
57. Through this Report, the Committee seeks to bring about structural changes and
capacity building in the present Ministry of Law and Justice by creating one more
Department in this Ministry, namely, Department of International Law as a part of legal
and judicial reforms. The Committee accordingly proposes that the Ministry should be
rechristened as Ministry of International Law, Domestic Law and Justice. The Committee
also suggests the following roadmap for strengthening the present Departments of Ministry
of Law and Justice:
(A) Department of Legal Affair: The appointment of Law Officers from the
Attorney General down to Prosecutors, and Government Advocates, Notary
Public should be looked through the prism of International Law for their
knowledge on International Law and practice. Some specialised Lawyers/legal
advisors are to be infused at various level in addition to refreshing the
existing nominees and appointees to get International Law exposure and
application in their day to day working. The Indian Law Institute (deemed
University) should have special courses in international law focussing on the
contemporary international law.  It is also suggested that Indian Society of
International Law (ISIL) Academy may be evolved into “Centre of Excellence”
in the field of International Law, as a pioneer institute in this field, if
necessary, through a Parliamentary enactment. The Committee wishes that
ISIL may be mandated for developing the human resources in the field of
ever growing Contemporary International law– –  by making, drafting,
interpreting, implementing and enforcing through sovereign State and the
three pillars of the Constitution of India, viz., the Parliament, the Executive
and the Judiciary.
(B) Legislative Department: The Legislative Department may strengthen the
existing Institute of Constitutional and Parliamentary studies (ICPS) by
shifting to allotted land in Chanakyapuri and remodel its syllabus and
curriculum of Legislative drafting in International Law and Domestic and
State Laws.

23
(C) Department of Justice: The Judiciary from Supreme Court down to the level
of Subordinate judiciary, Quasi Judicial Tribunals and adjudicative mechanism
are to be equipped with International Laws through National Judicial Academy
and State Judicial Academies. Sufficient financial support should be provided
by Union Government.

3. The Committee notes that for the year 2015-16, an allocation ` 562.99 crore has been made

Action T aken  by  the  Ministry/Department
3.1. The primary responsibility of infrastructure development for the subordinate judiciary rests with the
State Governments. The Central Government augments the resources of the State Governments by releasing
financial assistance under a centrally sponsored scheme for the development of judicial infrastructure. The
scheme has been in place since 1993-94, and was revised in 2011. It covers the construction of court
buildings and residential accommodation of judicial officers of district and subordinate courts. As of March,
2015, the Central Government had released an amount of ` 3,131 crore to the State Governments and UT
Administrations under the revised funding pattern from 2011-12 to 2014-15. This represents a significant
increase over the sum of ` 1,245 crore that was provided by the Central Government in the initial phase of
the scheme from 1993-94 to 2010-11. During the last financial year (2014-15), an amount of ` 933 crore
was released to the States.
3.2. Funds under the centrally sponsored scheme for development of infrastructural facilities for
judiciary are released to the States after obtaining the utilization certificates for the grants released in the
previous years as per the guidelines of the scheme. While examining the proposals received from the State
Governments, the projections made at the time of the revision of the scheme in 2011 for requirement of
funds for judicial infrastructure in the State for a time span of five years are also kept in view. The overall
release of funds during the financial year, however depends on the budgetary allocations made for the
scheme.

Recommendations  of  the  Committee
1. The Committee appreciates the initiative of National Mission for Justice Delivery and Legal Reforms.
The Committee however notes that only a token amount of ` 1 lakh has been made for it in BE (2015-16)
which implies that Ministry is still in the process of finalizing details of the Mission. The Committee finds it
rather shocking that a Mission started in 2011 with a time frame of five years has still not taken off. The
Committee desires the Ministry to ensure that the Mission is taken seriously and implemented in a time
bound manner and objectives of the Mission are achieved. [Para 6.33]
Action T aken  by  the  Ministry/Department
1.1. National Mission for Justice Delivery and Legal Reforms was set up in August, 2011 with the twin
objectives of increasing access by reducing delays and arrears in the system and enhancing accountability
through structural changes and by setting performance standards and capacities. The Mission has been
pursuing a co ordinated approach for phased liquidation of arrears and pendency in judicial administration,
which, inter-alia, involves better infrastructure for courts including computerisation, increase in strength
of subordinate judiciary, policy and legislative measures in the areas prone to excessive litigation, re-engineering
of court procedure for quick disposal of cases and emphasis on human resource development. 
1.2. The Mission has taken several steps in each of the strategic areas towards fulfilment of its objectives.
All States have formulated their Litigation Policies with a view to reduce the Governmental litigation. State
Governments have been requested to make an assessment of the impact of the State Litigation Policies on
controlling proliferation of litigation by State agencies. Department of Legal Affairs have formulated National
Litigation Policy, 2015, which is under active consideration of the Government.
 1.3. An Inter-Ministerial Group (IMG) was constituted to suggest necessary amendments to the Negotiable
Instruments (NI) Act along with other policy and administrative measures to check increasing litigation
relating to cheque bounce cases. The IMG has suggested a number of measures including procedural and
legislative changes to reduce number of cheque bounce cases. Policy and legislative changes have also been
recommended to tackle the large number of cases that are arising under the provisions of Motor Vehicles
Act, 1988 (MV Act). A Plan Scheme for Action Research and Studies on Judicial Reforms is being implemented
to inter-alia promote action research on judicial reforms. Five projects of Action Research have been sanctioned
so far under the scheme.
1.4. An important aspect of the judicial reforms relates to re-engineering court procedures and court
processes for early disposal of cases. Process service has been identified as a major bottleneck for timely
14

15
delivery of justice. A research note was prepared and circulated to High Courts for improving the process
service in civil and criminal matters. A positive response has been received from several High Courts on the
suggestions made in the research note. The subject matter of re-engineering of court process and case
management is also under active consideration of the National Court Management System (NCMS) of the
Supreme Court. Process re-engineering exercise is being carried out under e-Courts Mission Mode Project.
For promotion of alternative methods of dispute resolution, mediation centres are being set up in court
complexes at District and Taluka levels. Government agencies are being encouraged to include arbitration /
mediation clauses in government contracts.
1.5. Shortage of judicial officers / judges in district and subordinate courts is one of the main causes
for backlog and pendency of cases in courts. The National Mission has regularly pursued this matter with
the State Governments and the High Courts. As a result of the concerted efforts of all the stakeholders,
the sanctioned strength of judicial officers / judges in district and subordinate courts has increased from
17,715 at the end of 2012 to 20,214 in December, 2014. The mission is pursuing the matter with the High
Courts for filling up the existing vacancies. Emphasis is also being laid on proper training of all court
functionaries.
1.6. The primary responsibility of infrastructure development for the subordinate judiciary rests with the
State Governments. The Central Government augments the resources of the State Governments by releasing
financial assistance under a Centrally Sponsored Scheme (CSS) for development of judicial infrastructure.
Until 2011, the Central and State Governments used to contribute an equal share under the scheme but from
2011-12 onwards the fund-sharing pattern has been revised with the Central Government contributing 75%
of the funds. In case of States in the North-Eastern region, the Central Government provides 90% of the
funding. Central funding is, however, subject to budgetary allocation for the Scheme. As of March, 2015,
the Central Government has released an amount of `3131 crore to the State Governments and UT
administrations under the revised funding pattern from 2011-12 to 2014-15. This represents a significant
increase over the sum of `1,245 crore that was provided by the Central Government in the initial phase of
the scheme from 1993-94 to 2010-11.
1.7. Pendency reduction campaign was initiated for the first time in 2011. High Courts were requested to
prioritise disposal of cases that had been pending for a long duration, particularly those relating to senior
citizens and marginalised sections of society. In 2012 the focus of the campaign was to make the judicial
system free of cases that were over five years old. Pendency reduction campaign in 2013 focused on
weeding out ineffective and infructuous cases from the judicial system. In 2014 emphasis was laid on filling
up of vacancies of judicial officers and organization of Mega Lok Adalats. As a result of concerted efforts
made by various stakeholders the increasing trend of pendency of cases has been checked and the overall
pendency in subordinate courts has declined from 2.77 crore in 2010 to 2.64 crore in 2014. 
1.8. The establishment expenditure on National Mission is being met from the non-plan budget specifically
provided for the purpose. The budget head for National Mission Action Plan Implementation was created to
inter-alia undertake policy research activities to support the initiatives of National Mission. A technical
support cell was created for the National Mission under Access to Justice project being implemented in
partnership with UNDP. The budget for this purpose has been earmarked at `60.00 lakh under this project.
As such only a token provision of `1 lakh was made under the above budget head for the current financial
year. However the expenditure on e-Courts, construction of courts and residences for judges is also part of
the judicial reforms being undertaken by the Mission.

Recommendations  of  the  Committee
2. The Committee expresses its concern at the slow pace of establishment of Gram Nyalayas in different
States. It desires that the Department should review the entire issue in the light of experience gained and
expeditiously devise ways so that justice could be delivered to people at their door steps which is the basic
purpose of Gram Nayalayas Act, 2008. It may also focus on setting up of Gram Nayalayas in Talukas where
regular Courts have not been set up as decided in the Conference of Chief Justices of High Courts and Chief
Ministers of the States. [Para 6.48]
Action T aken  by  the  Ministry/Department
2.1. In terms of Section 3 (1) of the Gram Nyayalayas Act, 2008, it is for the State Governments to
establish Gram Nyayalayas in consultation with the respective High Courts. The issues affecting
operationalization of the Gram Nyayalayas were discussed in the Conference of Chief Justices of High
Courts and Chief Ministers of the States on 7th April, 2013. It was decided in the Conference that the State
Governments and High Courts should decide the question of establishment of Gram Nyayalayas wherever
feasible, taking into account their local problems. The focus is on setting up Gram Nyayalayas in the Talukas
where regular courts have not been set up.
Committee’s further observation
2.2 The  Committee  notes  the  reply.  The  Committee  feels  that  leaving  the  decision  to  establish
Gram Nyalayas entirely in the hands of State and concerned High Courts is a good step, which is a
step towards strengthening the federal structure of the Constitution. However , the Committee also
notes that it has led to uneven development/establishment of Gram Nyalayas in different  States in
the country and not a single Gram Nyalayas are operational in North Eastern States. Accordingly,
the  Committee  impress  upon  the  Department  to  explore  new  mechanisms/options  so  that  Gram
Nyalayas can be successfully established in various parts of the Country. The Committee recommends
that regular monitoring should be made to ensure that the States establish/operationalise, especially
in the North –Eastern States as not a single Gram Nyalayas are operational in these States.

Standing Committee on Personnel, Public Grievances, Law and Justice in its 78
th Report on the Demands for

Pensions in respect of the recommendations contained in the above mentioned Report, vide,  their
communications dated 20th  May, 2015,  9th June, 2015 and 28th July, 2016. These replies have been categorised
as follows :
Chapter – I : The recommendations/observations which have been accepted by the Ministry i.e., in
respect of paras 1.2., 2.4., 3.3., 4.2., 5.2., 6.2., 7.2., 8.2., 9.2., 10.3., 11.2., 12.5., 13.2., 14.5.15.2.,16.2.,

Chapter – II : The recommendations/observations which the Committee does not desire to pursue
in view of the replies given by the Ministry i.e.,  in respect of paras 33.2., 34.3., 35.3., 36.2., 37.2., 38.3.,
39.5., 40.2., 41.2., 42.3., 43.2., and 44.3.  of the Report. The Committee is convinced with the explanations

Chapter – III : The recommendations/observations in respect of which Committee has not accepted
replies given by the Ministry i.e., with regard to paras 45.3., 46.2., of the Report. The Committee expresses
its concern for not accepting the recommendations of the Committee dealt with in Chapter – III of this

Chapter – IV : The recommendations/observations in respect of which final replies of the Ministry
have not been received i.e., with regard to paras 47.2., 48.2. and 49.2.of the Report, the Committee observes

desires that the Ministry should furnish action taken notes in respect of the recommendations dealt with in

Recommendation/Observation

up of vacancies, the following steps have been taken which inter-alia include:-

with CAT for monitoring of the same to ensure speedy disposal of pending cases.

Protection of Whistle Blowers
Recommendation/observation
39. The Committee expresses its strong displeasure over non implementation of the Lokpal and Lokayuktas
Act, 2013 and the Whistle Blowers’ Protection Act. It is unfortunate that the Ministry has so far not taken
any steps to amend the Whistle Blowers Protection Act though it maintains that amendments are needed
before the Act can be implemented. The Committee recommends that the Ministry should take necessary
action for quick opprationalisation of both the Acts. (Para 3.10)
Action Taken Reply
39.1 The Whistle Blowers Protection Bill, 2011 was passed by the Lok Sabha on the 27th of December,
2011 and was transmitted to the Rajya Sabha. Subsequently, it was noticed that some of the provisions in the
Bill needed a relook with a view to strengthening the safeguards against disclosures which may prejudicially
21

22
affect the sovereignty and integrity of the country, security of the State, etc. Accordingly, notices for certain
official amendments were given to Rajya Sabha Secretariat from time to time. The Bill was finally taken up
for consideration and passing on 21st February, 2014. However, as the Bill was taken up on the last day of
the last Session of the 15th Lok Sabha, the official amendments which had been given notice of, were not
moved during consideration and passing of the Bill on the said date. The Bill was passed by the Rajya Sabha
without any amendments ( i.e., in the same form as passed by the Lok Sabha) on 21st February, 2014. The
Bill has received the assent of the President on 9th May, 2014 and has become the Whistle Blowers Protection
Act, 2011 (No. 17 of 2014). In view of this, the Whistle Blowers Protection Act, 2011 requires some
amendments (aimed at safeguarding against disclosures affecting sovereignty and integrity of India, security
of the State, etc.), before it is brought into force. To make these amendments to the Act, the Government
has introduced the Whistle Blowers Protection (Amendment) Bill, 2015 in the Lok Sabha on 11th May, 2015
which has been passed by the Lok Sabha on 13
th May, 2015. Notices are proposed to be issued for consideration
and passing of the said Bill in the Rajya Sabha during the ensuing Monsoon Session. Thus, the Department
has already taken action for expeditious implementation and enforcement of the Whistle Blowers Protection
Act, 2011. The same will be brought in force after the Parliament passes the aforesaid amendment Bill and
Presidential assent thereto is received.
39.2 The Lokpal and Lokayuktas Bill, 2011, after being passed by both the Houses of the Parliament has
become an Act titled “The Lokpal and Lokayuktas Act, 2013 (1 of 2014)” which was brought into force
with effect from 16
th January, 2014 vide notification of the same date. The Lokpal and Lokayuktas Act,
2013 requires some amendment so as to provide for situations where the composition of the Selection
Committee is deficient / incomplete due to absence of Leader of Opposition in the Lok Sabha, etc. Accordingly,
Lokpal & Lokayuktas and other related law (Amendment) Bill 2014 was introduced in Lok Sabha on 18.12.2014.
The same has been referred to the Parliamentary Standing Committee on Personnel, Public Grievances,
Law& Justice and is presently under consideration of the Committee. The Parliamentary Standing Committee
considering the Lokpal and Lokayuktas and other related Law (Amendment) Bill, 2014 has so far held its
meetings on the Bill on 08-01-2015, 03-03-2015, 08-04-2015, 15-04-2015 and 26.05.2015. Further one
more meeting has been scheduled for 16.07.2015. Besides this, the Standing Committee has also undertaken
study-visit on the said Bill to Kolkata, Mumbai, Hyderabad, Tirupati and Chennai from 14th to 23rd June,
2015 and to Srinagar from 10th July to 12th July, 2015. Further action can only be taken by the Government
after the Standing Committee submits its report on the said Bill.
Committee’s further observation
39.3 The Committee takes note of the reply.

INTRODUCTION
I, the Chairman of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Personnel, Public
Grievances, Law and Justice, having been authorised by the Committee to present the Report on its behalf,
do hereby present this Eighty-Fourth Report on Demands for Grants (2016-17) pertaining to the Ministry of
Law and Justice.
2. The Committee heard the Secretary, Department of Legal Affairs; Secretary, Legislative
Department; Secretary, Department of Justice; the Director-General, Election Commission of India;
the Registrar, Supreme Court; Secretary General, ICADR; Officiating Director, ICPS; Director, ILI;
Registrar, Appellate Tribunal for Foreign Exchange, Member Secretary, NALSA and Director, NJA
in its sitting held on the 29th March, 2016.
3. The Committee, while making its observations/recommendations, has relied upon the
following:-
(i) Detailed Demands for Grants of the Ministry for the year 2016-17;
(ii) Detailed Explanatory Notes on the Demands for Grants (2016-17) received from the
Ministry and the agencies and attached offices of the Ministry;
(iii) Annual Report of the Ministry for the year 2016-17 and the latest available Annual
Reports of the agencies and attached offices of the Ministry;
(iv) Written replies furnished by the Ministry to the Questionnaire sent to it by the
Secretariat;
(v) Written clarifications to the points/issues raised by Members in the meeting of the
Committee; and
(vi) Presentations made by the Secretary, Department of Legal Affairs; Secretary,
Legislative Department; Secretary, Department of Justice on 29th March, 2016; and
Director-General, Election  Commission of India;  Registrar,  Supreme  Court;
Secretary-General, ICADR; Officiating Director, ICPS; Director, ILI; Member,
Registrar, ATFE, Member Secretary, NALSA; and Director, NJA.
4. The Committee considered and adopted the Report in its sitting held on the 19th April, 2016.
5. For facility of reference and convenience, the observations and recommendations of the
Committee have been printed in bold letters in the body of the Report.

REPORT
CHAPTER - I
BRIEF OVERVIEW OF THE MINISTRY
1.0. The Union Ministry of Law and Justice comprises of three Departments, namely, the
Department of Legal Affairs, Legislative Department and Department of Justice and through the
said Departments, the Ministry assists in the process of orderly change directed towards realization
of the objectives set out in the Constitution.
DEPARTMENT OF LEGAL AFFAIRS
1.1. As per the Government of India (Allocation of Business) Rules, 1961, the Department of
Legal Affairs renders advice to various Ministries/Departments of the Government of India on legal
matters and carry out the litigation work in various Courts, including the Supreme Court. Besides
this, it is also concerned with the appointment of Law Officers, namely the Attorney General for
India, the Solicitor General of India and the Additional Solicitor Generals of India, assists in
entering into treaties with foreign countries in matters of civil law on behalf of the President of
India. It is also the nodal authority in respect of Appellate Tribunal for Foreign Exchange, the
Income Tax Appellate Tribunal and National Tax Tribunal.
1.2. The Department of Legal Affairs has a two tier set up, namely, the Main Secretariat at New
Delhi and the Branch Secretariats at Mumbai, Kolkata, Chennai and Bangalore. The nature of duties
discharged by the Main Secretariat and Branch Secretariats can be broadly classified into two areas
- Advice work and Litigation work. Advice caters to Central Government Departments/Offices at
Centre and in States/UTs and Litigation work relates to Central Administration Tribunal (CAT), High
Courts and Supreme Court.
1.3. The following are the organizations/institutions, which come under the overall supervision
of Department of Legal Affairs and get Grant-in-aid for their research works:-
(a) Law Commission of India: -  The Law Commission of India is a non-statutory
body, constituted by the Government once in three years. The Commission was first
constituted in 1955. It consists of a Chairman, three full-time Members, one
Member-Secretary and three or more part-time Members, depending upon the nature
of work. Law Commission Reports are considered to be primary source of law
reforms for Parliament, as well as the judiciary.
(b) Income Tax Appellate Tribunal (ITAT): -  Section 252 of the Income Tax Act,
1961 provides that the Central Government shall constitute an Appellate Tribunal
consisting of as many Judicial Members and Accountant Members as it thinks fit,
to exercise the powers and discharge the functions conferred on the Appellate
Tribunal by said Act.
(c) Appellate Tribunal of Foreign Exchange (ATFE): -  The Appellate Tribunal of
Foreign Exchange was established on 1
st June 2000 vide Government of India

2
Notification No. S.O. 531 (E), dated 1.6.2000 issued under section 18 of the
Foreign Exchange Management Act, 1999 (FEMA),
(d) Indian Law Institute (ILI):- The Indian Law Institute registered under the
Societies Registration Act, 1860 is engaged in research in the field of law.
(e) International Centre for Alternate Dispute Resolution (ICADR):- The
International Centre for Alternate Dispute Resolution was registered under the
Societies Registration Act, 1860 on 31
st May 1995. It is an autonomous organisation
working under the aegis of the Department.
(f) Bar Council of India (BCI): - The Bar Council of India is a statutory body
constituted under the Advocates Act 1961, which has been empowered among other
things to lay down standards of professional conduct and etiquette for lawyers,
maintain and improve the standard of legal education in the country.
(g) Institute of Constitutional and Parliamentary Studies (ICPS):-  The Institute of
Constitutional and Parliamentary Studies is a private body engaged in research in the
field of constitutional and parliamentary studies and came into existence in 1965.
LEGISLATIVE DEPARTMENT
1.4. The Legislative Department acts mainly as a service provider in so far as the legislative
business of the Union Government is concerned. The Department is entrusted with legislative
matters and is responsible for drafting of all Government Bills and Ordinances and scrutiny and
vetting of subordinate legislations sponsored by various Union Ministries/ Departments. Rendering
assistance to Parliament and Joint/Standing Committees in respect to Bills before its enactment. It
is also administratively concerned with certain matters such as the Code of Civil Procedure,
Limitation and Arbitration, Contracts, Personal Laws, Evidence and Transfer of Property. There are
over hundred Central Acts falling under these subjects.
1.5. The Department has two wings under it mainly:-
(i) Institute of Legislative Drafting and Research : With a view to increase the
availability of trained legislative draftsmen in the country, the Institute of Legislative
Drafting and Research was established as a Wing of the Legislative Department,
Ministry of Law and Justice in January, 1989.
(ii) Official Languages Wing and Vidhi Sahitya Prakashan : The Official Languages
Wing is a successor Organisation of the Official Languages (Legislative) Commission
under the Legislative Department. It has been entrusted with the preparation and
publication of a standard legal terminology for use in all Official Languages;
authoritative texts in Hindi of all Central Acts and Ordinances and Regulations
promulgated by the President, all rules, regulations and orders made by the Central
Government under any Central Act and authoritative texts of all Central Acts and
Ordinances and Regulations promulgated by the President in the respective Official
Languages of the States and to arrange for the translation of all Acts passed and
Ordinances promulgated in any State into Hindi, if the texts of such Acts or
Ordinances are in a language other than Hindi.

3
1.6 Election Commission of India:  Legislative Department is also administratively concerned
with the Election Commission of India and Election laws connected with election to Parliament and
State Legislatures and to the offices of the President and the Vice-President. There is a separate
Demand No.55 for the Election Commission of India.
DEPARTMENT OF JUSTICE
1.7. The duties of the Department of Justice, as per the Government of India (Allocation of
Business) Rules, 1961, include the administration of justice and the processing of appointment of
judges of the Supreme Court and High Courts, appointment of Judicial Commissioners and Judicial
Officers in Union Territories, creation of All India Judicial Service and extension/exclusion of the
jurisdiction of a High Court to a Union Territory.
1.8. The following institutions/autonomous bodies/policy initiatives come directly under the
overall supervision of Department of Justice:
(a) Supreme Court of India:-  There is a separate demand No.57 (Appropriation)
pertaining to the Supreme Court of India. The expenditure to be incurred on the
Supreme Court of India is ‘Charged’
 expenditure .
(b) National Legal Services Authority (NALSA):-  The National Legal Services
Authority has been constituted under the Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987 to
monitor and evaluate implementation of legal aid programmes and to lay down
policies and principles for making legal services available under the Act. The NALSA
issues guidelines for the State Legal Services Authorities to implement the legal aid
programmes which are in turn discharged through the following services:-
(i) Free Legal Services: It includes court fees, process fee and all charges
payable or incurred in connection with any legal proceedings, providing
Advocate in legal proceedings, etc.
(ii) Lok Adalats: -  Lok Adalat is a forum where the disputes/cases pending in
the court of law or at pre-litigation stage are settled/compromised amicably.
The Lok Adalat has been given statutory status under the Legal Services
Authorities Act, 1987.
(c) Family Courts/Special Courts :- The Family Court Act, 1984 was enacted with a
view to providing for establishment of Family Courts, to promote conciliation and
secure speedy settlement of disputes relating to marriage, family affairs and related
matters. In accordance with the provisions of section 3 of the Act, the State/UT
Governments can establish Family Courts in the areas comprising districts, towns,
city in the States having population of ten lakhs. Even the States/UTs are competent
to establish such court in those areas with the State/UT having a population less
than ten lakhs in consultation with the concerned High Court.
(d) National Judicial Academy :- The National Judicial Academy was registered as a
Society under the Societies Registration Act and came into existence with effect
from 17
th August, 1993. The affairs of the Academy are managed by a Governing

4
Council, which is chaired by the Chief Justice of India. The registered office of the
Academy is in Supreme Court Building at New Delhi and another office was
established in August, 2000 at Bhopal. The main objectives of the Academy are to
impart training to the Judicial Officers of the States/Union territories and to study
the court management and administration of justice in States and Union territories.
(e) Centrally Sponsored Scheme: The Government is implementing a Centrally
Sponsored Scheme (CSS) for development of infrastructure facilities for judiciary
since 1993-94. The scheme covers construction of court buildings and residential
accommodation of judicial officers/judges covering only Subordinate courts. Under
the Scheme, funds are provided to the States to augment their capacities for
infrastructure development of the District and Subordinate Courts. The modified
CSS is to be implemented in a Mission Mode approach over the years 2011-16 under
the National Mission.
(f) National Mission for Justice Delivery and Legal Reforms:  Set up for five years
in 2011, and became fully functional with effect from the financial year 2012-13.
The twin goals of the Mission include increasing access by reducing delays and
arrears in the system and enhancing accountability at all levels through structural
changes and setting performance standards and facilitating enhancement of
capacities for achieving such performance standards. The four schemes proposed to
be pursued under the Mission are as under;
(a) Scheme for Computerization of the District and Subordinate Courts / E-
Courts.
(b) Access to Justice - Government of India.
(c) Strengthening of Access to Justice in India (SAJI (EAP).
(d) Action Research and Studies on Judicial Reforms.
(g)   Access to Justice- Externally Aided Project (UNDP assisted)
The Project started in 2009 with support under the United Nations Development
Programme (UNDP). The Project is being implemented in 7 States (Bihar,
Chhattisgarh, Jharkhand, Madhya Pradesh, Odisha, Rajasthan and Uttar Pradesh) and
aims to strengthen access to justice for the marginalized - particularly women,
scheduled castes, scheduled tribes and minorities - by supporting strategies and
initiatives that seek to address the barriers they face.
 (h) Access to Justice- North-East and Jammu and Kashmir (Government of India
Project)
The Project started in 2012 and covers the 12
th Five year Plan period (2012-2017)
to venture in those regions of the Country which have so far been under-represented
and unheard in the arena and discourses of Access to Justice. The project aims to
make Justice accessible to the marginalised sections of the society. The project aims
to train lawyers, law students and customary judicial officers to raise awareness

5
among people about their legal rights. It is hoped that the project will be a milestone
in establishing a model of access to justice in remote areas of North East Region
and Jammu & Kashmir.
(i)    Computerization of District and Subordinate Courts E-courts Mission Mode
Project Phase-I & II :- This is a scheme proposed in the 12
th Plan with components
such as computerisation of 1000 new Courts, use of solar energy under e-Courts
Project, computerisation of the Public Prosecutors Office, videoconferencing facility
for jails, enhancement of ICT infrastructure of courts, digitization of old case
records, computerisation of Judicial libraries, up-gradation of application software,
SMS based services, Touch Screen Kiosks with a provision of ` 1280 crore which
would spread over a period of five years.
(j) Establishment of Gram Nyayalayas under the Gram Nyayalayas Act, 2008 :-
The Gram Nyayalayas Act, 2008 has been enacted by the Parliament to provide for
the establishment of the Gram Nyayalayas at the grass root level for the purpose of
providing speedy and inexpensive access to justice to the citizens at their door steps.
The Central Government would meet 50% of the recurring expenses to be incurred
on the setting up of these courts in the first three years subject to a ceiling of
` 3.20 lakhs per annum.
(k) The Fourteenth Finance Commission  has recommended ` 9,749 crore to the
Department of Justice for pendency reduction by establishing additional courts, Fast
Track Courts, establishment of Family Courts, redesigning existing courts to make
them litigant-friendly, augmenting technical support for e-courts, scanning and
digitalization, Access to justice- legal aid, Lok Adalats, ADR, Training and capacity
building of judges, public prosecutors, mediators and lawyers and establishing state
judicial academies for Manipur, Meghalaya and Tripura.

CHAPTER – II

(ii) Demand No. 56  is the consolidated Budget Estimates pertaining to the Department

(iii) Demand No. 57  pertains to the Supreme Court of India, which is under the

Supreme Court of India is ‘charged’ expenditure.

CHAPTER - III
DEMAND NO. 55: ELECTION COMMISSION OF INDIA
3.0. The entire expenditure of the Election Commission of India (ECI) is ‘ voted ’. The BE
and RE  for 2015-16 was ` 80 and ` 85.29 crore respectively whereas the BE for 2016-17
is ` 121.52 crore.
AN ANALYSIS OF THE BUDGET ESTIMATES
3.1. The BE of 2016-17 of the Election Commission of India exceeds the RE (2015-16) by
` 36.23 crore. The RE for the financial year 2015-16 was ` 85.29 crore including ` 17.00 crore
for the construction of India International Institute of Democracy and Election
Management (IIIDEM) campus. The voted grants for the financial year 2016-17 is ` 121.52 crore,
which includes the provision of ` 40.00 crore granted as capital expenditure for construction of
IIIDEM campus. In the Capital Section, there has also been an increase from ` 17.00 crore in RE
2015-16 to ` 40.00 crore BE 2016-17. The ECI in its written submission on the Demands for
Grants (2016-17) to the Committee submitted that the 51.91 percent and 42.48 percent upward
variation in BE 2016-17 over BE 2015-16 and BE 2016-17 over RE 2015-16 is mainly due to
increase in provision for the construction of IIIDEM campus.
3.2. The Committee was appraised that the increase of ` 36.23 crore from Revised Estimate
(2015-2016) in Budget Estimate (2016-17) are mainly due to increase in Professional service

3.12. V oter-verified paper audit trail (VVPAT) is a method of providing feedback to voters using
a ballot less voting system. Under VVPAT, a printer-like apparatus is linked to Electronic V oting
Machine (EVM). When a vote is cast, a receipt is generated showing the serial number, name and
symbol of the candidate. It confirms the vote and the voter can verify the details.
3.13. The Commission submitted that EVMs are produced by two public sector units, i.e. BEL
and ECIL. These are the only two units which are authorized to produce it and have the expertise
and all the securities relating to EVMs. So, EVMs and VVPATs are the two machines which are

15
